headline: A US appeals court ruled that a legal-research company broke copyright law by training its AI on Thomson Reuters' Westlaw material.
score_reason: Headline overstated: the ruling is narrow (non-generative AI, verbatim copying), and the ruling is from last week.
importance_line: It is the first appeals-court ruling on AI training and fair use, which matters to authors, publishers and AI developers, but it concerns a non-generative tool that copied text verbatim, so its reach to chatbots is doubtful.
summary: Futurism reports that the US Third Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a ruling that Ross Intelligence, a legal-search start-up that shut down in 2021, broke copyright law by training its search engine on Thomson Reuters' Westlaw material, mainly short editorial summaries called headnotes that it copied almost verbatim; Futurism, citing Reuters, calls it the first such appeals ruling, decided last week. Legal commentator Aaron Moss says the case is a poor test for chatbots like ChatGPT because Ross's AI was not generative and damages are unresolved; Ross's remnants plan to appeal to the Supreme Court, and a hearing in Concord Music Group's lyrics lawsuit against Anthropic is due later this month.
freshness: FOLLOW-UP of the week of 28 Sep 2026
notes: Ruling date not given ('last week'); Reuters, which Futurism cites for 'first of its kind', was not read. Headline of the source overstates the holding.
